newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-WasteMan sees future in water.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-WasteMan sees future in water.

text.p: Waste Management NZ Ltd is setting its long-term sights on diversification into water supply and treatment, Chief Executive Kim Ellis said.
Ellis said there appeared little scope for acquisitions and limited opportunities for landfill south of Auckland, where local authorities were keen to retain their monopolies.
"So it's water business we are chasing," he said.
The company was recently voted the Deloitte/Management company of the year, which Ellis said probably arose from its ability to take a long-term view.
"My brief is to maintain the momentum and to look out into the future," Ellis said in an interview.
"One of the reasons for our success is that we've got the Redvale landfill (in Auckland) -- a strategic asset -- now generating earnings, but the work went into it five years before," he said.

The company had an opportunity in Wellington, which would not be enormous in terms of profit but important stategically. Waste Management has a bid in with the Wellington City Council for a biosolids contract and has a "50/50" chance of success. Anglian Water has the contract for the treatment plant.
"We're down to the last two and they are going to make a decision in the next two weeks. That may take a year and a half to gain consent and a year and a half to construct.
"There are the profit streams out there for the next regime of managers in Waste Management.
"The industry is not really growing a lot so we are having to create some of that opportunity by going into the privatisation process with councils and so on.
"You've got to take yourself away for 30 percent of the time and focus on the long-term stuff which could generate nothing for the bonus this year, otherwise the thing runs out of steam."
Ellis said waste volumes, over time, would not increase.
Auckland was more of an international scale market with greater scope for growth and more private participation in landfill programmes.
Core earnings at present come from waste collection fees, but landfill operations enabled the company to vertically integrate in Auckland.
By the end of March 1997, Waste Management will have spent NZ$40 million on Redvale.
The company recently won a contract from Thames Coromandel for water and waste water reticulation and treatment. There were also opportunities for Auckland's Watercare sludge treatment.
Given the industry's current limitations, Ellis said the focus would be on getting more out of existing businesses.
"It's about leveraging off the asset base. We are the major player here so we've got to do better out of what we get out of our people and our customer base.
"And then it's the five-year outlook -- how we are going to crank some more business out of the market in new areas."
Waste Management NZ is 60 percent owned by Waste Management International Plc (WMI), which in turn is 80 percent owned by WMX Technologies Inc in the U.S.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
